newsitem.title: USA: You're young, sharp and up to your eyeballs in debt.
newsitem.headline: You're young, sharp and up to your eyeballs in debt.

text.p: Congratulations, graduates. By now, you've probably got the diploma, a week's worth of beach tan and the please-hire-me grin.
Oh, and one other thing -- a five-figure debt burden.

According to recent surveys, 1997's college graduates have an average debt of $11,500, and that's just for college loans. It does not include car loans, money owed to parents for educational expenses and credit card bills for ... whatever.

Not only that, but you're losing your roommates and the Student Loan Marketing Association -- the purchaser of most school loans known as Sallie Mae -- wants you. If you haven't already been notified that you're supposed to start repaying those loans within six months, you soon will be.
What can you do about it? Here are some tips.

- First, don't despair. Almost everyone leaves school feeling, and in many cases actually being, poor. With a little luck, a little money management and some time on your side, you'll be able to catch up and prosper financially.

- Remember that credit cards are poison unless you really understand how they work and have the discipline to use them, instead of the other way around. Issuers love nothing more than to press cards on young people entering their acquisitive years. But every month that you charge more than you can pay delays by many months your eventual day of financial freedom.

To best manage your credit, keep a no-fee card for convenience and pay it off in full every month. If you find yourself having to finance a bigger purchase, like a job hunter's wardrobe or a refrigerator, find the lowest-interest rate card you can to make that purchase.

- Take some time to study the student loan repayment options that suit you best. Sally Mae offers several. For example, if you used a standard repayment option on that $11,500, at today's rates, you'd have monthly payments of $141 for 10 years.

With a two-year so-called graduated repayment plan, you'd pay only $79 a month for two years and $164 a month for the next seven years. Another plan would have you paying $79 a month for four years and then $203 in the fifth year.

Which is better? With the graduated plans, you'll pay more over the long term, but if money is tight now, use them and then prepay early if you get that big raise in two or three years. And at 8.25 percent, the interest rates you're paying are better than you would pay on many other loans.

- Whatever option you choose, make your payments on time. If you make the first four years worth of monthly payments on time, Sallie Mae will cut your interest rate by 1 percentage point, to an effective rate of 7.25 percent. If you authorise Sallie Mae to go into your checking account and automatically deduct monthly payments, you shave another quarter point off the rate.

- Abandon pre-conceived notions of what "adults" have. Just because you're embarking on real life doesn't mean you need a new car or even a car at all. Or an apartment all to yourself. In fact, living like a student for another year or two is one of the fastest ways to burn that debt and get on your feet financially.

- Find health insurance. Once you graduate college, you typically lose your parents' plan. Even a not very serious injury could put a crimp in your finances for some time. Save money by getting a good quality, high deductible, catastrophic policy and sweating the small stuff yourself.

- Try, as hard as it is, to save. The more money you can save, the less dependent you will ever be on a job you don't like. And remember this: if you stash away just $20 a week, every week, you can have $50,000 tucked away when you're 40 and ready to go back to school.
And believe me, some day you will be 40.
